title: Agent Memory and Planning
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Agent Memory and Planning ##### The assistant that asked the same question 47 times A team in Hyderabad built an internal engineering assistant. Useful, well-received, and it had one behaviour that quietly drove people away. Every session, it asked which team you were on. Every session, it asked whether you preferred Python or Go examples. Every session, it re-explained their deployment pipeline from scratch because it did not know you had asked about it yesterday. One engineer's logs showed the assistant asking "which environment are you deploying to?" **47 times across six weeks** — always answered "staging", always forgotten. Their memory implementation was the conversation buffer: the last ten turns, discarded at session end. That is short-term memory, and it is the only kind most agents have. Adding a long-term store — a small set of durable facts per user, retrieved at session start — took two days. Session length dropped 34% because users stopped re-explaining context, and satisfaction scores moved more than any model upgrade had. **Memory is what turns a stateless tool into something that accumulates value from use.** Today is the architecture: what to store, how to retrieve it, and — the part people skip — what to forget. ##### The memory taxonomy ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Agent memory"] --> B["Working memory
current task scratchpad"] A --> C["Short-term
this conversation"] A --> D["Long-term"] D --> E["Episodic
what happened, when"] D --> F["Semantic
facts and preferences"] D --> G["Procedural
learned how-to"] B -.->|"discarded at task end"| X["ephemeral"] C -.->|"summarised into"| D E -.->|"generalised into"| F ``` | Type | Holds | Lifetime | Storage | |---|---|---|---| | **Working** | Tool calls, intermediate results | One task | Agent state (Day 26) | | **Short-term** | Recent turns | One session | Message list, trimmed | | **Episodic** | "On 12 March the user deployed to staging and hit ERR_4021" | Months | Vector store, timestamped | | **Semantic** | "User is on the payments team, prefers Go" | Indefinite | Key-value store | | **Procedural** | "This user's deploy flow: build → stage → smoke test" | Indefinite | Structured records | **The Hyderabad system had only the second row.** Semantic memory — a handful of stable facts — was what it needed, and it is the cheapest kind to add. ##### Short-term: managing the window Conversation history grows, costs grow quadratically (Day 31's point), and eventually the window overflows. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass import tiktoken @dataclass class ConversationBuffer: """Token-budgeted history with rolling summarisation.""" max_tokens: int = 6000 keep_recent_turns: int = 6 model: str = "gpt-4o-mini" def __post_init__(self): self.enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o") self.messages: list[dict] = [] self.summary: str = "" def _count(self, msgs) -> int: return sum(len(self.enc.encode(m["content"])) for m in msgs) def add(self, role: str, content: str, llm=None): self.messages.append({"role": role, "content": content}) if self._count(self.messages) > self.max_tokens and llm: self._compress(llm) def _compress(self, llm): """Summarise the older half, keep recent turns verbatim.""" keep = self.messages[-self.keep_recent_turns:] older = self.messages[:-self.keep_recent_turns] if not older: return transcript = "\n".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content']}" for m in older) self.summary = llm( f"Previous summary:\n{self.summary or '(none)'}\n\n" f"New exchanges to fold in:\n{transcript}\n\n" f"Write an updated summary preserving: decisions made, facts the user " f"stated, unresolved questions, and any identifiers mentioned. " f"Under 250 words." ) self.messages = keep def render(self, system_prompt: str) -> list[dict]: msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}] if self.summary: msgs.append({"role": "system", "content": f"Earlier in this conversation:\n{self.summary}"}) return msgs + self.messages ``` **Rolling summarisation beats truncation** because it preserves decisions and stated facts. Plain truncation drops the turn where the user said "I'm on the payments team" and the agent asks again three turns later. **Preserve identifiers explicitly in the summary prompt.** Summarisation is where ticket numbers and error codes get paraphrased into "the error the user mentioned" — the same failure as Day 22's query rewriting. ##### Semantic memory: durable facts The Hyderabad fix. A small set of extracted, stable facts about the user. ```python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import Literal from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() class MemoryFact(BaseModel): key: str = Field(..., description="snake_case identifier, e.g. 'team'") value: str category: Literal["identity", "preference", "context", "constraint"] confidence: Literal["stated", "inferred"] supersedes: bool = Field(False, description="True if this replaces a prior value") class ExtractedMemories(BaseModel): facts: list[MemoryFact] EXTRACT_SYSTEM = """Extract durable facts about the user from this conversation. Extract ONLY facts that will still be true next week: - identity: team, role, systems they own - preference: language, verbosity, format - context: current project, environment they work in - constraint: things they cannot do or must avoid Do NOT extract: - Transient state ("I'm debugging right now") - The content of their question - Anything you inferred weakly confidence: 'stated' if the user said it explicitly, 'inferred' otherwise. supersedes: true if this contradicts something likely stored before.""" def extract_memories(conversation, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> list[MemoryFact]: transcript = "\n".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content']}" for m in conversation[-20:]) completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=ExtractedMemories, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": EXTRACT_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": transcript}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed.facts ``` ```python import json import time from pathlib import Path class SemanticMemory: """Key-value facts per user, with provenance and update history.""" def __init__(self, store_path="memory/semantic.json"): self.path = Path(store_path) self.path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) self.data = json.loads(self.path.read_text()) if self.path.exists() else {} def upsert(self, user_id: str, fact: MemoryFact): user = self.data.setdefault(user_id, {}) existing = user.get(fact.key) # Do not let a weak inference overwrite something the user stated if existing and existing["confidence"] == "stated" and fact.confidence == "inferred": return False user[fact.key] = { "value": fact.value, "category": fact.category, "confidence": fact.confidence, "updated_at": time.time(), "previous": existing["value"] if existing else None, } self._save() return True def render(self, user_id: str, categories=None) -> str: user = self.data.get(user_id, {}) items = [(k, v) for k, v in user.items() if not categories or v["category"] in categories] if not items: return "" return "What I know about this user:\n" + "\n".join( f"- {k.replace('_', ' ')}: {v['value']}" for k, v in sorted(items)) def forget(self, user_id: str, key: str): """DPDP Act erasure — must actually work.""" self.data.get(user_id, {}).pop(key, None) self._save() def forget_user(self, user_id: str): self.data.pop(user_id, None) self._save() def _save(self): self.path.write_text(json.dumps(self.data, indent=2)) ``` **The stated-versus-inferred rule prevents a real failure.** An agent that infers "prefers brief answers" from one short exchange should not overwrite the user's explicit "I want detailed explanations." **Keep semantic memory small.** Ten to thirty facts per user, injected into every system prompt. It costs a few hundred tokens per call and eliminates the re-asking problem entirely. Anything larger belongs in episodic memory, retrieved on demand. **`forget_user` must actually delete.** Under the DPDP Act 2023 a user can require erasure, and a memory system with no deletion path is a compliance problem, not just an engineering gap. ##### Episodic memory: retrieval over history Facts are few and always relevant. Episodes are many and situationally relevant, so they go in a vector store. ```python import numpy as np import time from datetime import datetime class EpisodicMemory: """Timestamped events, retrieved by relevance and recency.""" def __init__(self, vectorstore, embedder, collection="episodes"): self.vs = vectorstore self.embedder = embedder self.collection = collection def record(self, user_id: str, event: str, kind: str, metadata=None): ts = time.time() eid = f"{user_id}::{int(ts * 1000)}" self.vs.upsert( ids=[eid], documents=[event], metadatas=[{"user_id": user_id, "kind": kind, "timestamp": ts, "date": datetime.fromtimestamp(ts).strftime("%Y-%m-%d"), **(metadata or {})}], ) return eid def recall(self, user_id: str, query: str, k=5, recency_half_life_days=30.0, recency_weight=0.3): """Score = relevance × (1-w) + recency × w.""" res = self.vs.query( query_texts=[query], n_results=k * 4, where={"user_id": user_id}, include=["documents", "metadatas", "distances"], ) if not res["ids"][0]: return [] now = time.time() half_life_s = recency_half_life_days * 86400 scored = [] for doc, meta, dist in zip(res["documents"][0], res["metadatas"][0], res["distances"][0]): relevance = 1 - dist age = now - meta["timestamp"] recency = 0.5 ** (age / half_life_s) combined = relevance * (1 - recency_weight) + recency * recency_weight scored.append({"event": doc, "metadata": meta, "relevance": round(relevance, 3), "recency": round(recency, 3), "score": round(combined, 4)}) return sorted(scored, key=lambda x: -x["score"])[:k] ``` **Exponential recency decay is the key detail.** A highly relevant episode from eight months ago is usually less useful than a moderately relevant one from last week, and a pure similarity search cannot express that. The Stanford generative-agents paper used a similar relevance-recency-importance combination. **Record episodes selectively.** Logging every turn produces a store full of noise. Record decisions, errors encountered, tasks completed, and corrections the user made — the events that would inform future behaviour. ##### Reflection: episodic to semantic The mechanism that lets memory improve rather than merely accumulate. Periodically review recent episodes and derive generalisations. ```python class Reflection(BaseModel): insights: list[str] = Field(..., description="Generalisations from the episodes") new_facts: list[MemoryFact] REFLECT_SYSTEM = """Review these recent interactions with a user and derive durable insights. Look for: - Recurring patterns in what they ask about - Preferences revealed by their corrections - Systems or projects they consistently work with - Approaches that worked or failed for them Produce insights that would improve future interactions. Be specific and grounded in the episodes — do not speculate.""" def reflect(user_id, episodic: EpisodicMemory, semantic: SemanticMemory, n_recent=25, model="gpt-4o-mini"): episodes = episodic.recall(user_id, query="recent activity", k=n_recent, recency_weight=0.9) if len(episodes) < 5: return None text = "\n".join(f"[{e['metadata']['date']}] {e['event']}" for e in episodes) completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.3, response_format=Reflection, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": REFLECT_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Recent interactions:\n{text}"}], ) result = completion.choices[0].message.parsed for fact in result.new_facts: semantic.upsert(user_id, fact) return result ``` **Run reflection asynchronously**, not in the request path — it is a background job triggered every N interactions or nightly. Doing it inline adds seconds to a user-facing response for a benefit that is not needed until the next session. ##### Forgetting The part almost nobody implements, and the reason memory systems degrade. ```python class MemoryMaintenance: """Decay, deduplicate, and prune. Memory that only grows becomes noise.""" def __init__(self, semantic: SemanticMemory, episodic: EpisodicMemory, embedder): self.semantic, self.episodic, self.embedder = semantic, episodic, embedder def prune_stale_facts(self, user_id, max_age_days=180, protect_categories=("identity", "constraint")): """Remove old inferred facts; keep stated identity and constraints.""" user = self.semantic.data.get(user_id, {}) now = time.time() removed = [] for key, fact in list(user.items()): if fact["category"] in protect_categories: continue if fact["confidence"] == "stated": continue if (now - fact["updated_at"]) / 86400 > max_age_days: del user[key] removed.append(key) self.semantic._save() return removed def deduplicate_episodes(self, user_id, threshold=0.94): """Collapse near-identical episodes, keeping the most recent.""" all_eps = self.episodic.vs.query( query_texts=[""], n_results=1000, where={"user_id": user_id}, include=["documents", "metadatas"]) docs = all_eps["documents"][0] if len(docs) < 2: return 0 emb = self.embedder.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True) sims = emb @ emb.T np.fill_diagonal(sims, 0) to_delete = set() order = np.argsort([-m["timestamp"] for m in all_eps["metadatas"][0]]) for i in order: # newest first if i in to_delete: continue dupes = np.where(sims[i] > threshold)[0] to_delete.update(int(d) for d in dupes if d != i) ids = [all_eps["ids"][0][i] for i in to_delete] if ids: self.episodic.vs.delete(ids=ids) return len(ids) ``` **Protect stated identity and constraints from decay.** "User cannot access production" is a constraint that should never expire on a timer. **Deduplicate keeping the newest.** If a user has told you their team seven times, the most recent statement is the authoritative one. ##### Planning and decomposition Memory tells the agent what it knows; planning tells it what to do. ```python from typing import Optional class PlanStep(BaseModel): id: str description: str depends_on: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list) tool: Optional[str] = None success_criteria: str class TaskPlan(BaseModel): goal: str steps: list[PlanStep] estimated_steps: int PLAN_SYSTEM = """Break the task into concrete, verifiable steps. Rules: - Each step must be independently checkable via its success_criteria. - Use depends_on for steps that need an earlier step's output. - Prefer 3-7 steps. Fewer means the steps are too coarse; more means over-planning. - Name the tool each step needs, or null if it is reasoning only. - Use what you already know about the user to avoid asking redundant questions.""" def create_plan(task, user_context, available_tools, model="gpt-4o"): completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=TaskPlan, messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": PLAN_SYSTEM + f"\n\nAvailable tools: {', '.join(available_tools)}"}, {"role": "user", "content": f"{user_context}\n\nTask: {task}"}, ], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed ``` **Passing `user_context` from memory into planning is what closes the loop.** The planner that knows the user is on the payments team and deploys to staging does not generate a step asking which environment. **Replanning** on failure matters more than the initial plan: ```python def execute_with_replanning(plan: TaskPlan, executor, max_replans=2): completed, failed = {}, [] for attempt in range(max_replans + 1): remaining = [s for s in plan.steps if s.id not in completed] for step in remaining: if not all(d in completed for d in step.depends_on): continue result = executor(step, completed) if result["success"]: completed[step.id] = result["output"] else: failed.append({"step": step.id, "reason": result["error"]}) break if len(completed) == len(plan.steps): return {"status": "complete", "results": completed, "replans": attempt} if attempt < max_replans: plan = replan(plan, completed, failed) return {"status": "incomplete", "results": completed, "failed": failed} ``` ##### Assembling the memory-augmented agent ```python class MemoryAugmentedAgent: def __init__(self, semantic, episodic, buffer, planner, executor, llm): self.semantic, self.episodic = semantic, episodic self.buffer, self.planner, self.executor, self.llm = buffer, planner, executor, llm def build_context(self, user_id: str, task: str) -> str: """Assemble memory into a bounded context block.""" parts = [] facts = self.semantic.render(user_id) if facts: parts.append(facts) episodes = self.episodic.recall(user_id, task, k=4) if episodes: parts.append("Relevant past interactions:\n" + "\n".join( f"- [{e['metadata']['date']}] {e['event']}" for e in episodes)) return "\n\n".join(parts) def handle(self, user_id: str, task: str) -> dict: context = self.build_context(user_id, task) plan = self.planner(task, context, self.executor.tool_names) result = execute_with_replanning(plan, self.executor) answer = self.llm( f"{context}\n\nTask: {task}\n\n" f"Results:\n{result['results']}\n\nWrite the response.") self.episodic.record( user_id, event=f"Task: {task}. Outcome: {result['status']}.", kind="task", metadata={"status": result["status"]}) for fact in extract_memories(self.buffer.messages): self.semantic.upsert(user_id, fact) return {"answer": answer, "plan": plan, "result": result, "context_used": bool(context)} ``` **Bound the memory context.** Semantic facts plus four episodes is a few hundred tokens; unbounded retrieval of twenty episodes crowds out the actual task. Set a token budget and stay inside it. ##### Common mistakes - **Only conversation buffers**, so nothing survives the session — the 47 questions. - **Truncating history** instead of summarising, losing stated facts. - **Summarisation that paraphrases away identifiers.** - **No forgetting**, so memory accumulates contradictions and noise. - **Letting inferred facts overwrite stated ones.** - **No deletion path**, which is a DPDP Act compliance gap. - **Reflection in the request path**, adding seconds of latency. - **Unbounded episodic retrieval**, crowding out the task. - **Recording every turn** rather than decisions and outcomes. - **Memory not passed into planning**, so the planner re-asks known things. - **No recency weighting**, surfacing stale episodes over recent ones. - **Storing PII in episodic memory** without redaction — Day 40's concerns apply. ##### Hands-on: make it remember across sessions Your practical task adds long-term memory to an agent with a vector store, retrieval, and periodic summarisation. The test that matters is cross-session: run a conversation, end it, start a fresh session with the same user ID, and verify the agent knows what you told it. Then check the negative case — a new user ID should get no leaked context. The mini project builds a personal assistant that remembers preferences and plans multi-step tasks. Implement all three memory types and log which ones contributed to each response. Then run the maintenance job and report what it pruned and deduplicated — a memory system without maintenance degrades within weeks, and demonstrating the maintenance is what shows you understand that. The assignment designs a memory architecture specifying what is stored, retrieved, and forgotten. **The forgetting policy is the part that distinguishes a real design.** Specify retention by category, what is protected from decay, the deduplication threshold, and the user-initiated erasure path. Include the token budget for injected memory, because an architecture that does not bound its context will eventually break the agent it serves. ##### Key takeaways - **Short-term memory is what most agents have; long-term memory is what makes them useful** — a handful of durable facts eliminates the re-asking problem entirely. - **Separate semantic facts from episodic events.** Facts are few and always injected; episodes are many and retrieved by relevance combined with exponential recency decay. - **Never let an inferred fact overwrite a stated one**, and preserve identifiers explicitly when summarising. - **Reflection turns episodes into facts** — run it as a background job, not in the request path. - **Forgetting is a feature.** Decay stale inferences, protect stated constraints, deduplicate, and implement genuine user-initiated erasure.
practical_task_reference: Add long-term memory to an agent using a vector store, with retrieval and periodic summarization.
